poor comprehenders recruit different brain areas than healthy seniors with good comprehension, and that the poor comprehenders use an alternate processing strategy for grammatically complex information.

healthy seniors with poor comprehension have significantly reduced recruitment of brain regions previously associated with sentence comprehension and verbal working language, and increased activation of brain regions previously not associated with sentence comprehension.

the neural bases of sentence comprehension and the cognitive and brain mechanisms underlying the development of language comprehension deficits.

the poor comprehenders demonstrated a compensatory pattern of brain recruitment for the grammatically simple sentences that they understood, and a reduced pattern of brain recruitment, compared to the healthy controls, for the grammatically complex sentences that they did not understand.

poor sentence comprehension in the elderly is associated with decreased activation of the left perilesional network, which includes Broca's area, and increased activation of the right perilesional network.

the left perislvian regions are important for grammatically guided processing in subjects with poor comprehension, while other regions are recruited in these subjects for alternate strategies.
